grammar.case.ablative.help: The ablative answers questions such as with what, by what, where and when, often after prepositions like in, cum, ab and ex: “in īnsulā” (on the island), “cum amīcō” (with a friend).
grammar.case.ablative.label: ablative
grammar.case.accusative.help: The accusative is the case of the direct object, the person or thing that receives the action: in “puella rosam videt” (the girl sees the rose), rosam is accusative. It also follows prepositions of motion such as ad and in (into).
grammar.case.accusative.label: accusative
grammar.case.dative.help: The dative is the case of the indirect object, the person to whom or for whom something is done: in “puellae dōnum dat” (gives a gift to the girl), puellae is dative.
grammar.case.dative.label: dative
grammar.case.genitive.help: The genitive shows that something belongs to or is part of something else, like “of” in English: “liber Mārcī” (the book of Marcus, Marcus’s book).
grammar.case.genitive.label: genitive
grammar.case.locative.help: The locative says where something is with names of cities and a few words such as domī (at home): “Rōmae” (in Rome).
grammar.case.locative.label: locative
grammar.case.nominative.help: The nominative is the case of the subject, the person or thing that does the action: in “puella cantat” (the girl sings), puella is nominative. It is also the dictionary form of nouns.
grammar.case.nominative.label: nominative
grammar.case.vocative.help: The vocative is the case used to call or speak to someone directly: “Mārce, venī!” (Marcus, come!). For most words it looks like the nominative.
grammar.case.vocative.label: vocative
grammar.degree.comparative.help: The comparative compares two things: “bigger, more beautiful”: maior, pulchrior.
grammar.degree.comparative.label: comparative
grammar.degree.positive.label: positive
grammar.degree.superlative.help: The superlative means “the most” or “very”: pulcherrimus (the most beautiful, very beautiful).
grammar.degree.superlative.label: superlative
grammar.gender.common.label: common gender
grammar.gender.feminine.help: Feminine is one of the three genders of nouns. Adjectives that describe a feminine noun take feminine endings: rosa pulchra (a beautiful rose).
grammar.gender.feminine.label: feminine
grammar.gender.feminineNeuter.label: feminine or neuter
grammar.gender.masculine.help: Masculine is one of the three genders of nouns. Adjectives that describe a masculine noun take masculine endings: lupus magnus (a big wolf).
grammar.gender.masculine.label: masculine
grammar.gender.masculineFeminine.label: masculine or feminine
grammar.gender.masculineNeuter.label: masculine or neuter
grammar.gender.neuter.help: Neuter is the third gender, neither masculine nor feminine. In neuter words the nominative and accusative always look the same: caelum serēnum (a clear sky).
grammar.gender.neuter.label: neuter
grammar.mood.gerund.help: The gerund is a verb form used like a noun: ars legendī (the art of reading).
grammar.mood.gerund.label: gerund
grammar.mood.gerundive.help: The gerundive is a verb form used like an adjective that often means “to be done”: liber legendus (a book to be read).
grammar.mood.gerundive.label: gerundive
grammar.mood.imperative.help: The imperative gives orders and requests: vidē! (see!), venīte! (come, all of you!).
grammar.mood.imperative.label: imperative
grammar.mood.indicative.help: The indicative is the mood of facts and real events: puella rosam videt (the girl sees the rose).
grammar.mood.indicative.label: indicative
grammar.mood.infinitive.help: The infinitive is the form of the verb that names the action without a person, like “to see”: vidēre.
grammar.mood.infinitive.label: infinitive
grammar.mood.optative.help: The optative is a Greek mood for wishes and for possibilities: ἴδοι (may she see).
grammar.mood.optative.label: optative
grammar.mood.participle.help: A participle is a verb form used like an adjective, with case, number and gender: puella cantāns (the singing girl).
grammar.mood.participle.label: participle
grammar.mood.subjunctive.help: The subjunctive is the mood of wishes, possibilities, purposes and many subordinate clauses: videat (may she see, so that she sees).
grammar.mood.subjunctive.label: subjunctive
grammar.mood.supine.help: The supine is a rare verb form that shows purpose after verbs of motion: spectātum venit (she comes to watch).
grammar.mood.supine.label: supine
grammar.number.dual.help: The dual is a number of Greek for exactly two persons or things, such as a pair of eyes or two friends. Latin has no dual.
grammar.number.dual.label: dual
grammar.number.plural.help: Plural means more than one: rosae (roses).
grammar.number.plural.label: plural
grammar.number.singular.help: Singular means one person or thing: rosa (one rose).
grammar.number.singular.label: singular
grammar.person.first.help: First person is the speaker: “I” in the singular, “we” in the plural: videō (I see).
grammar.person.first.label: first person
grammar.person.second.help: Second person is the one spoken to: “you”: vidēs (you see).
grammar.person.second.label: second person
grammar.person.third.help: Third person is someone or something else: “he, she, it, they”: videt (she or he sees).
grammar.person.third.label: third person

grammar.tense.aorist.help: The aorist is a Greek past tense for a single, completed action, without stressing how long it lasted: εἶδε (she saw).
grammar.tense.aorist.label: aorist
grammar.tense.future.help: The future tells what will happen: vidēbit (she will see).
grammar.tense.future.label: future
grammar.tense.futurePerfect.help: The future perfect tells about an action that will be finished before a moment in the future: vīderit (she will have seen).
grammar.tense.futurePerfect.label: future perfect
grammar.tense.imperfect.help: The imperfect tells what was going on or used to happen in the past, without saying when it ended: vidēbat (she was seeing, she used to see).
grammar.tense.imperfect.label: imperfect
grammar.tense.perfect.help: The perfect tells about a finished action in the past: vīdit (she saw, she has seen).
grammar.tense.perfect.label: perfect
grammar.tense.pluperfect.help: The pluperfect tells about an action finished before another past action: vīderat (she had seen).
grammar.tense.pluperfect.label: pluperfect
grammar.tense.present.help: The present tells what happens now or usually happens: videt (she sees, she is seeing).
grammar.tense.present.label: present
grammar.voice.active.help: In the active voice the subject does the action: puella videt (the girl sees).
grammar.voice.active.label: active voice
grammar.voice.middle.help: The middle voice is a Greek voice in which the subject acts on itself or for itself: λούομαι (I wash myself).
grammar.voice.middle.label: middle voice
grammar.voice.passive.help: In the passive voice the subject receives the action: puella vidētur (the girl is seen).
grammar.voice.passive.label: passive voice
